newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Indonesia cocoa due to arrive in Brazil next week.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia cocoa due to arrive in Brazil next week.

text.p: Brazil's port of Ilheus is to receive next week the first of an anticipated 15,000 tonnes of cocoa to be imported up to August because a shortfall in the midcrop, said an official at one of the importing companies.

The first shipment of 4,000 tonnes is being brought in by a pool of three firms - Joanes Industria (a subsidiary of the U.K's E.D. and F. Man), Chadler and the Brazilian arm of Swiss food giant Nestle SA.

The cocoa is from Indonesia, currently the only producing country which has been pre-certified as free of risk by the Brazilian government following new rules set down after the problematic purchase of 5,000 tonnes of Ivorian beans in 1995.

The pool is negotiating a further 6,000 tonnes, likely also to come from Indonesia, and has already requested the Agriculture Ministry conduct a risk survey of the Ivory Coast as another optional origin, the company official said.
The Agriculture Ministry gave the go-ahead to the Indonesian imports after the industry reached a consensus with producers over a supply shortfall at the start of the Bahian midcrop.

The midcrop, normally harvested between May and September, is expected only to begin from the end of this month with a forecast harvest of between 900,000 and one million 60-kg bags, said National Cocoa Producers Council head Wallace Setenta.

Based on current crop estimates, producers agreed there could be a deficit of up to 250,000 60-kg bags (15,000 tonnes) and gave their blessing to imports to prevent processing facilities standing idle due to a shortage of raw materials.
Normally the beans would be subject to a 10 percent import tax but the cocoa is being brought in on a drawback basis with an agreement to export an equivalent amount of products.
There are currently talks amongst the various sectors on the possibility of reducing the 10 percent bean tax as well as the 12 percent import tax on products, traders and producers said.

"These shipments are just the first step. At the moment we'll be looking optimistically at a 1997/98 crop of around three million bags but processors can handle six million bags and installed capacity could be up to 10 million," one dealer said.

"We're looking at production of less and less beans to the extent that soon the industry may have to import to supply the internal market and if that is the case, there is every reason to want to reduce import taxes," he added.
